claim: Ribosome biogenesis consumes up to 40% of the cell's energy in rapidly growing Escherichia coli.
source: Ribosome biogenesis, which consumes up to 40% of the cell's energy in rapidly growing Escherichia coli (Maguire, 2009), involves the coordinated transcription, modification, and folding of rRNA transcripts; translation, modification, and folding of r-proteins; binding of r-proteins to the appropriate rRNA scaffolds; and binding and release of ribosome biogenesis factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maguire, 2009.

claim: E. coli has approximately 60 ribosome biogenesis factors.
source: E. coli has approximately 60 of such factors.
evidence: The claim is stated as a fact in the manuscript text and draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Genetic defects in ribosome assembly result in cold sensitive growth phenotypes.
source: Indeed, numerous studies have revealed that genetic defects in ribosome assembly result in cold sensitive growth phenotypes (Bryant and Sypherd, 1974; Dammel and Noller, 1995; Jones et al., 1996; Bubunenko et al., 2006; Connolly et al., 2008; Clatterbuck Soper et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: More than 20% of ribosome-related genes in the Keio collection are cold sensitive.
source: This normalization procedure highlighted ribosome-related genes as exceptionally sensitive to low temperatures, as >20% of genes in this functional class were found to be cold sensitive.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the Keio collection screen shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The proportion of cold sensitive genes in the translation class (21%) is statistically significant.
source: By permuting the classification assignments, we determined that the proportion of cold sensitive genes in the translation class (21%) was significant with a bootstrapped p-value < 1e−6.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the Keio collection screen data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lamotrigine increases in potency more than 50-fold from >512 μM at 37°C to 7.8 μM at 15°C.
source: The anticonvulsant drug lamotrigine displayed the largest change in minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) upon temperature downshift, increasing in potency more than 50-fold from >512 μM at 37°C to 7.8 μM at 15°C (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment with lamotrigine results in the accumulation of non-native ribosomal particles after 1 hr of incubation.
source: Treatment with lamotrigine resulted in the accumulation of non-native ribosomal particles after 1 hr of incubation and did so in a time-dependent manner (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose density gradient data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Treatment of E. coli with 2× MIC of lamotrigine for only 5 min causes a significant accumulation of non-native particles.
source: Further investigations revealed that treatment of E. coli with 2× MIC of lamotrigine for only 5 min (∼1% of the doubling time) caused a significant accumulation of these non-native particles (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose density gradient data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: Pre-30S and pre-50S particles that accumulate at 15°C are not present after treatment at 37°C.
source: Consistent with the cold sensitive phenotype induced by lamotrigine, these pre-30S and pre-50S particles that accumulated at 15°C were not present after treatment at 37°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose density gradient data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Lamotrigine does not interact directly with mature or non-native ribosomal particles.
source: Radiolabeled compound was found exclusively in the soluble fractions eluting early in the gradient, suggesting that lamotrigine does not interact directly with mature or non-native ribosomal particles.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from [3H]-lamotrigine localization experiments described in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Inhibitors of protein translation can cause accumulation of immature ribosomal particles.
source: Since previous reports have shown that inhibitors of protein translation can cause accumulation of immature ribosomal particles (Siibak et al., 2009, 2011; Sykes et al., 2010), we also tested a panel of antibiotics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D) with known mechanism of action for comparison.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cultures treated with chloramphenicol, erythromycin, and tetracycline display a substantial accumulation of non-native ribosomal particles after just 1 hr of treatment.
source: Cultures treated with chloramphenicol (Figure 3B), erythromycin (Figure 3C), and tetracycline (Figure 3D) displayed a substantial accumulation of non-native ribosomal particles after just 1 hr of treatment, illustrating that inhibition of translation can indirectly inhibit ribosomal subunit assembly by limiting the availability of r-proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose density gradient data shown in Figure 3B, 3C, and 3D.

claim: Inhibition of translation can indirectly inhibit ribosomal subunit assembly by limiting the availability of r-proteins.
source: Cultures treated with chloramphenicol (Figure 3B), erythromycin (Figure 3C), and tetracycline (Figure 3D) displayed a substantial accumulation of non-native ribosomal particles after just 1 hr of treatment, illustrating that inhibition of translation can indirectly inhibit ribosomal subunit assembly by limiting the availability of r-proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed effects of translation inhibitors on ribosome assembly.

claim: The cleavage of 5′ and 3′ termini of rRNA is among the final events in ribosomal subunit assembly.
source: Because previous investigations have shown that the cleavage of 5′ and 3′ termini of rRNA is among the final events in ribosomal subunit assembly (Lindahl, 1973; Mangiarotti et al., 1974; Srivastava and Schlessinger, 1988), we first performed 5′ primer extension reactions using rRNA purified from sucrose gradients of lamotrigine-treated cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lamotrigine treatment results in the accumulation of immature 16S rRNA in the pre-30S region.
source: The quantity of immature 16S rRNA from DMSO-treated cells was minor relative to cells treated with lamotrigine.
evidence: The claim is supported by 5′ primer extension data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The major species of rRNA residing within the pre-30S region in lamotrigine-treated cells is unprocessed 16S rRNA.
source: These results indicate that, by far, the major species of rRNA residing within the pre-30S region in lamotrigine-treated cells was unprocessed 16S rRNA.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative cDNA fluorescence data from 5′ primer extension reactions shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Lamotrigine treatment results in the accumulation of an immature 30S subunit that sediments at ∼25S and an immature 50S subunit that sediments at ∼40S.
source: Thus, 5′ primer extension results strongly suggested that lamotrigine treatment results in the accumulation of an immature 30S subunit that sediments at ∼25S and an immature 50S subunit that sediments at ∼40S.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from 5′ primer extension data shown in Figure 4.

claim: S2, S3, and S21 are the latest-binding small subunit proteins.
source: The depletion of these proteins is consistent with prior in vivo analysis of small subunit biogenesis at 37°C, which found S2, S3, and S21 to be the latest-binding small subunit proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C; Chen and Williamson, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chen and Williamson, 2013 and mass spectrometry data.

claim: Lamotrigine treatment results in the accumulation of an immature large subunit particle depleted of late-binding r-proteins L35, L36, L16, L30, and L28 as well as earlier-binding proteins L34, L6, and L21.
source: Inspection of large subunit protein occupancy revealed drastic changes as a result of lamotrigine treatment, resulting in the accumulation of an immature particle depleted of the late-binding r-proteins L35, L36, L16, L30, and L28 as well as earlier-binding proteins, L34, L6, and L21 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The 30S-specific maturation factor RbfA co-sediments with the 30S particles in both DMSO- and lamotrigine-treated samples.
source: The 30S-specific maturation factor RbfA co-sedimented with the 30S particles in both DMSO- and lamotrigine-treated samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The 50S-biogenesis factor DeaD co-migrates with the pre-50S peak in the lamotrigine-treated samples and the 50S peak in the DMSO-treated samples.
source: Further, the 50S-biogenesis factor DeaD co-migrated with the pre-50S peak in the lamotrigine-treated samples and the 50S peak in the DMSO-treated samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The pre-30S and pre-50S particles are immature subunits and not the result of degradation of mature ribosomal particles.
source: These data further suggest that the pre-30S and pre-50S particles are immature subunits and not the result of degradation of mature ribosomal particles.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the presence of ribosome biogenesis factors RbfA and DeaD in the pre-30S and pre-50S particles.

claim: All spontaneous suppressor mutations blocking lamotrigine activity map solely to domain II of translation initiation factor IF2.
source: Spontaneous suppressor mutations blocking lamotrigine activity mapped solely to the poorly characterized domain II of translation initiation factor IF2 and prevented the binding of lamotrigine to IF2 in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data of suppressor mutants described in the Results section.

claim: Suppressor mutations in IF2 prevent the binding of lamotrigine to IF2 in vitro.
source: Spontaneous suppressor mutations blocking lamotrigine activity mapped solely to the poorly characterized domain II of translation initiation factor IF2 and prevented the binding of lamotrigine to IF2 in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All mutations in suppressor strains mapped to domain II of IF2 and fell into only four categories.
source: Subsequent Sanger sequencing of the infB genes from each of the remaining 17 suppressor strains revealed that all mutations mapped to domain II of IF2 and fell into only four categories.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data of suppressor strains.

claim: Three classes of suppressor mutants contained in-frame chromosomal deletions in domain II of IF2 and one mutant class contained a short duplication.
source: Three classes of mutant contained in-frame chromosomal deletions in this region and one mutant class contained a short duplication.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data of suppressor strains shown in Figure 5A.

claim: All suppressor strains displayed wild-type growth at 15°C in the absence of lamotrigine and little sensitivity to lamotrigine treatment up to 512 μM in LB media.
source: All displayed wild-type growth at 15°C in the absence of lamotrigine and little sensitivity to lamotrigine treatment up to 512 μM in LB media (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve and potency analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Treatment of suppressor strains with lamotrigine did not result in the accumulation of non-native ribosomal particles.
source: Treatment of suppressor strains with lamotrigine did not result in the accumulation of non-native ribosomal particles (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose density gradient data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lamotrigine binds to wild-type E. coli IF2 in a G-nucleotide-dependent manner, with lamotrigine-IF2 complex formation favored in the presence of GDP over GTP.
source: Lamotrigine was found to associate with wild-type E. coli IF2 in a G-nucleotide-dependent manner, with lamotrigine-IF2 complex formation favored in the presence of GDP over GTP (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Lamotrigine does not bind to mutant IF2 in the presence of GTP and GDP.
source: Analyses of lamotrigine binding with mutant IF2 in the presence of GTP and GDP failed to reveal association (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Lamotrigine has activity solely against members of the Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Consistent with these results, lamotrigine was found to have activity solely against members of the Enterobacteriaceae (Supplementary file 2), which is the only bacterial family that contains the domain II sequence outlined in Figure 5A.
evidence: The claim is supported by potency analysis data across different bacterial species shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The Enterobacteriaceae is the only bacterial family that contains the domain II sequence of IF2 outlined in Figure 5A.
source: Consistent with these results, lamotrigine was found to have activity solely against members of the Enterobacteriaceae (Supplementary file 2), which is the only bacterial family that contains the domain II sequence outlined in Figure 5A.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The potency of lamotrigine at 15°C against the Enterobacteriaceae is directly correlated with IF2-α sequence homology.
source: Interestingly, the potency of lamotrigine at 15°C against the Enterobacteriaceae was directly correlated with IF2-α sequence homology, further suggesting that the sequence of domain II defines essential structural features for lamotrigine association (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment and potency data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Lamotrigine has no impact on [35S]-methionine incorporation, even when cells are treated with 8× MIC of lamotrigine.
source: These investigations revealed that lamotrigine had no impact on [35S]-methionine incorporation, even when cells were treated with 8× MIC of lamotrigine (Figure 6A, C, black dots).
evidence: The claim is supported by [35S]-methionine incorporation assay data shown in Figure 6A and 6C.

claim: Cells treated with 8× MIC of lamotrigine at 37°C for three doublings do not display any inhibition of translation.
source: Similarly, cells treated with these same concentrations of lamotrigine at 37°C for three doublings did not display any inhibition of translation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by [35S]-methionine incorporation assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells treated with 8× MIC of tetracycline, chloramphenicol, and erythromycin show a marked decrease in protein labeling.
source: We found that when cells were treated with 8× MIC of tetracycline, chloramphenicol, and erythromycin, there was a marked decrease in protein labeling.
evidence: The claim is supported by [35S]-methionine incorporation assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cells treated with 8× MIC of vancomycin do not display inhibition of protein biosynthesis after 2.6 hr of treatment.
source: As expected given its known mechanism of action, cells treated with 8× MIC of vancomycin did not display inhibition of protein biosynthesis after 2.6 hr of treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by [35S]-methionine incorporation assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Lamotrigine fails to block the production of luciferase at either 15°C or 37°C in cell-free translation assays.
source: Lamotrigine failed to block the production of luciferase at either 15°C or 37°C (Figure 6B, C, white dots, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-free translation assay data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Evernimicin prevents luciferase synthesis in vitro at both 15°C and 37°C.
source: Evernimicin prevented luciferase synthesis in vitro at both 15°C and 37°C (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-free translation assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Evernimicin is an oligosaccharide antibiotic known to inhibit IF2-dependent 70S initiation complex formation.
source: To ensure that the in vitro translation assay required IF2 activity, we tested the effect of evernimicin, an oligosaccharide antibiotic known to inhibit IF2-dependent 70S initiation complex formation (McNicholas et al., 2000; Belova et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McNicholas et al., 2000 and Belova et al., 2001.

claim: Each ribosomal protein is synthesized at a similar rate in DMSO- and lamotrigine-treated cells up to 6× MIC.
source: Using a linear approximation of the synthesis rate based on the 4-, 8-, and 16-hr time points, we found that each protein was synthesized at a similar rate in the DMSO- and lamotrigine-treated cells up to 6× MIC.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry-based pulse labeling data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There is significant inhibition of r-protein synthesis with increasing concentrations of chloramphenicol.
source: However, we found significant inhibition of r-protein synthesis with increasing concentrations of chloramphenicol, our positive control compound (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,H,J, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry-based pulse labeling data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells relieved of lamotrigine stress assemble immature 30S and 50S particles into mature 30S and 50S subunits.
source: We hypothesized that cells relieved of lamotrigine stress would assemble immature 30S and 50S particles into mature 30S and 50S subunits.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis that is tested by the pulse-chase experiment shown in Figure 7.

claim: After removal of lamotrigine and non-labeled uridine chase, the levels of pre-30S and pre-50S particles decrease with a corresponding increase in 70S ribosomes.
source: Some 30 min after removal of lamotrigine and non-labeled uridine chase, the relative proportions of ribosomal particles began to adjust. Specifically, the levels of pre-30S and pre-50S particles decreased with a corresponding increase in 70S ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase experiment data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: After 3 hr of chase, there are no apparent differences between DMSO-treated and lamotrigine-treated cells.
source: This trend continued throughout the 3-hr chase period, after which there were no apparent differences between DMSO-treated and lamotrigine-treated cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase experiment data shown in Figure 7.

claim: After 1 hr of non-labeled uridine chase, a cluster of three particles that sedimented at approximately 40S, 45S, and 50S appear.
source: Interestingly, after 1 hr of non-labeled uridine chase, a cluster of three particles that sedimented at approximately 40S (discussed above as the pre-50S), 45S, and 50S appeared.
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase experiment data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: With each successive time point, the levels of 50S increase at the expense of the 40S and 45S particles, suggesting cells are actively assembling the pre-50S particles into 50S subunits.
source: With each successive time point, the levels of 50S increased at the expense of the other particles, suggesting our time course had captured cells actively assembling the pre-50S particles into 50S subunits.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from pulse-chase experiment data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Lamotrigine is a widely available chemical probe of bacterial ribosome biogenesis.
source: This work establishes lamotrigine as a widely available chemical probe of bacterial ribosome biogenesis and suggests a role for E. coli IF2 in ribosome assembly.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: E. coli IF2 has a role in ribosome assembly.
source: This work establishes lamotrigine as a widely available chemical probe of bacterial ribosome biogenesis and suggests a role for E. coli IF2 in ribosome assembly.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that IF2 is the target of lamotrigine and that lamotrigine affects ribosome assembly.

claim: The bacterial ribosome is a 2.6-MDa ribonucleoprotein complex responsible for protein translation.
source: The bacterial ribosome is a 2.6-MDa ribonucleoprotein complex responsible for protein translation, which sediments as a 70S particle composed of a small (30S) and a large (50S) subunit.
evidence: The claim is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: The bacterial ribosome sediments as a 70S particle composed of a small (30S) and a large (50S) subunit.
source: The bacterial ribosome is a 2.6-MDa ribonucleoprotein complex responsible for protein translation, which sediments as a 70S particle composed of a small (30S) and a large (50S) subunit.
evidence: The claim is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis factors are proteins that transiently bind to assembling ribosomal particles to increase the efficiency of subunit maturation.
source: Ribosome biogenesis factors are proteins that transiently bind to assembling ribosomal particles to increase the efficiency of subunit maturation (Bunner et al., 2010) and prevent the entry of immature subunits into the translation cycle (Strunk et al., 2011; Boehringer et al., 2012; Lebaron et al., 2012; Strunk et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis factors prevent the entry of immature subunits into the translation cycle.
source: Ribosome biogenesis factors are proteins that transiently bind to assembling ribosomal particles to increase the efficiency of subunit maturation (Bunner et al., 2010) and prevent the entry of immature subunits into the translation cycle (Strunk et al., 2011; Boehringer et al., 2012; Lebaron et al., 2012; Strunk et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Small molecules can exert their effects on a time scale of seconds and be added or removed from cell systems at will.
source: Such chemicals can exert their effects on a time scale of seconds and be added or removed from cell systems at will.
evidence: The claim is a statement of general knowledge about small molecules as research tools.

claim: Small molecules can be dosed to achieve varying levels of target inhibition.
source: Further, small molecules can be dosed to achieve varying levels of target inhibition and as such can be elegant probes of protein function.
evidence: The claim is a statement of general knowledge about small molecules as research tools.

claim: No chemical probes exist for the study of ribosome biogenesis.
source: While existing antibiotics provide a surfeit of probes for on-going efforts to understand the mechanistic details of protein translation, no chemical probes exist for the study of ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Chemical inhibitors of bacterial ribosome biogenesis might serve as leads for an entirely new mechanistic class of antibiotics.
source: Additionally, chemical inhibitors of bacterial ribosome biogenesis might serve as leads for an entirely new mechanistic class of antibiotics (Comartin and Brown, 2006).
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: The doubling time of wild-type E. coli at 15°C in LB media is 6 hr.
source: We note that the doubling time of wild-type E. coli at 15°C in LB media was 6 hr.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observation.

claim: Immature ribosomal particles in unperturbed cells account for only a small proportion of total ribosomal material.
source: This is consistent with previous reports, which have shown that immature ribosomal particles in unperturbed cells account for only a small proportion of total ribosomal material (Mulder et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Domain II of IF2 is conserved solely among IF2 proteins from the Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Interestingly, domain II is conserved solely among IF2 proteins from the Enterobacteriaceae and has yet to be assigned a definitive function.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Domain II of IF2 has yet to be assigned a definitive function.
source: Interestingly, domain II is conserved solely among IF2 proteins from the Enterobacteriaceae and has yet to be assigned a definitive function.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: One study suggests a role for domain II of IF2 in binding strongly to 30S, 50S, and 70S ribosomal particles relative to the other Enterobacteriaceae IF2 domains.
source: Indeed, only one study suggests a role for this region in binding strongly to 30S, 50S, and 70S ribosomal particles relative to the other Enterobacteriaceae IF2 domains (Moreno et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moreno et al., 1999.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, eIF5B associates with immature 40S subunits in a translation-like checkpoint, wherein immature 40S particles bind to mature 60S subunits prior to final maturation.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, eIF5B associates with immature 40S subunits in a translation-like checkpoint, wherein immature 40S particles bind to mature 60S subunits prior to final maturation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lebaron et al., 2012 and Strunk et al., 2012 mentioned earlier in the context of eIF5B.

claim: Overexpression of IF2 in a ΔyjeQ background of E. coli partially suppresses the mutant slow growth phenotype and restores ribosome profiles to wild type.
source: Interestingly, our observations help rationalize the previously unexplained finding that overexpression of IF2 in a ΔyjeQ background of E. coli partially suppresses the mutant slow growth phenotype and restores ribosome profiles to wild type (Campbell and Brown, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Campbell and Brown, 2008.

claim: The 30S particles of cells lacking YjeQ display significantly depleted occupancy of S21, S1, S2, and S3.
source: Similarly to lamotrigine-treated cells, the 30S particles of cells lacking YjeQ display significantly depleted occupancy of S21, S1, S2, and S3 (Jomaa et al., 2011), suggesting that IF2 may perform an overlapping role in late 30S maturation during cold stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jomaa et al., 2011.

claim: IF2 may perform an overlapping role in late 30S maturation during cold stress.
source: Similarly to lamotrigine-treated cells, the 30S particles of cells lacking YjeQ display significantly depleted occupancy of S21, S1, S2, and S3 (Jomaa et al., 2011), suggesting that IF2 may perform an overlapping role in late 30S maturation during cold stress.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the similarity between lamotrigine-treated cells and ΔyjeQ cells.

claim: Truncation of the N-terminus of E. coli IF2, containing domain II, leads to cold sensitive growth.
source: Our results also parallel work dating back almost two decades, which showed that truncation of the N-terminus of E. coli IF2, containing domain II led to cold sensitive growth (Laalami et al., 1991a, 1991b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Laalami et al., 1991a and 1991b.

claim: Much of the machinery involved in ribosome biogenesis is conserved among bacteria and eukaryotes.
source: With much of the machinery involved in ribosome biogenesis (Bharat et al., 2006; Schaefer et al., 2006) and translation (Anger et al., 2013) conserved among bacteria and eukaryotes, the maintenance of IF2/eIF5B function in ribosome biogenesis through evolution is surely plausible.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bharat et al., 2006 and Schaefer et al., 2006.

claim: Much of the machinery involved in translation is conserved among bacteria and eukaryotes.
source: With much of the machinery involved in ribosome biogenesis (Bharat et al., 2006; Schaefer et al., 2006) and translation (Anger et al., 2013) conserved among bacteria and eukaryotes, the maintenance of IF2/eIF5B function in ribosome biogenesis through evolution is surely plausible.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Anger et al., 2013.

claim: The maintenance of IF2/eIF5B function in ribosome biogenesis through evolution is plausible.
source: With much of the machinery involved in ribosome biogenesis (Bharat et al., 2006; Schaefer et al., 2006) and translation (Anger et al., 2013) conserved among bacteria and eukaryotes, the maintenance of IF2/eIF5B function in ribosome biogenesis through evolution is surely plausible.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the conservation of ribosome biogenesis and translation machinery.

claim: Lamotrigine may perturb late steps in 30S and 50S subunit assembly.
source: With these regions encompassing the functional centers of each subunit, it is tempting to speculate that lamotrigine may perturb late steps in 30S and 50S subunit assembly.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the observation that immature subunits lack r-proteins in functional centers.

claim: The functional centers of ribosomal subunits are among the last sites to mature.
source: It has recently been suggested that these sites are among the last to mature (Jomaa et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Jomaa et al., 2014) consistent with this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: A bacterial model may include association of two immature particles prior to maturation of the functional centers within the 30S and 50S subunits.
source: Given that pre-30S and pre-50S particles accumulate during lamotrigine stress, a bacterial model may include association of two immature particles prior to maturation of the functional centers within the 30S and 50S subunits.
evidence: The claim is a speculative model proposed based on the observed accumulation of immature particles.

claim: It is possible that IF2 is involved in the maturation of 30S and 50S subunits independently.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that IF2 is involved in the maturation of 30S and 50S subunits independently.
evidence: The claim is a speculative alternative model.

claim: The data strongly support a central role for the enigmatic and divergent domain II of E. coli IF2 in the assembly of both subunits.
source: Regardless of the precise events mediated by IF2, our data strongly support a central role for the enigmatic and divergent domain II of E. coli IF2 in the assembly of both subunits.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Domain II may have a purpose that is uniquely important to the Enterobacteriaceae under cold stress.
source: Domain II may have a purpose that is uniquely important to the Enterobacteriaceae under cold stress or, alternatively, species-specific proteins that mimic the N-terminus of IF2 from Enterobacteriaceae may perform this activity.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis about the function of domain II.

claim: Species-specific proteins that mimic the N-terminus of IF2 from Enterobacteriaceae may perform the activity of domain II in other bacterial species.
source: Domain II may have a purpose that is uniquely important to the Enterobacteriaceae under cold stress or, alternatively, species-specific proteins that mimic the N-terminus of IF2 from Enterobacteriaceae may perform this activity.
evidence: The claim is a speculative alternative hypothesis.

claim: Lamotrigine will serve as an important tool in expanding our understanding of the molecular details of IF2 in ribosome biogenesis.
source: We posit that lamotrigine will serve as an important tool in expanding our understanding of the molecular details of IF2 in ribosome biogenesis and functions as a proof-of-concept molecule in the development of novel antibiotics.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about the future utility of lamotrigine.

claim: Lamotrigine functions as a proof-of-concept molecule in the development of novel antibiotics.
source: We posit that lamotrigine will serve as an important tool in expanding our understanding of the molecular details of IF2 in ribosome biogenesis and functions as a proof-of-concept molecule in the development of novel antibiotics.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about the potential application of lamotrigine.
